opus-5.5.text:
Sure. I think the bear case is roughly this: scaling has been running on a pretty steep exponential in compute spending, something like 3-5x per year on the biggest training runs, and that's only sustainable if revenue keeps up. Right now, the big labs and hyperscalers are spending far more on data centers and training than AI is bringing in. That's fine if investors believe the revenue curve will eventually catch up, but it means the whole thing depends on confidence.

So the scenario I'd worry about if I were bearish goes like this. The next generation or two of models come out, and they're better, but not dramatically better in ways that translate into money. Agents are still somewhat unreliable, so companies can't actually replace large chunks of labor. Revenue keeps growing, maybe even quickly in percentage terms, but not fast enough to justify the next 10x in capex. At that point you'd see some tightening. Investors get more skeptical, the hyperscalers start caring more about margins, and maybe one of the smaller labs struggles to raise its next round. Then the growth rate of compute investment slows from tripling per year to something more modest.

Beyond that, there are real physical constraints that hit around the same time: power, fab capacity, the lead times on building gigawatt-scale data centers. Even if the money were there, you can't always deploy it quickly. So you could get a situation where scaling continues, but at maybe half the pace people were extrapolating, and that matters a lot for timelines.

That said, I don't find the bear case all that compelling as my median view. Revenue at the leading labs has been growing really fast, and you don't need AI to be transformative across the whole economy to justify a lot of spending. You need it to be very valuable in a few domains, and software engineering already looks like a strong candidate. Also, the people writing the checks, like Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon, have enormous cash flows and see this as close to existential competitively, so they're willing to tolerate losses for a long time.

So my overall take is that I'd put maybe a 25-35% chance on some meaningful financial slowdown in the next few years, where the scaling rate drops noticeably. But even in that world, I don't think progress stops. Algorithmic progress continues, inference compute keeps getting cheaper, and you'd probably just push timelines back by a few years rather than fundamentally changing the picture. The thing that would really update me toward the bear case is if we see a couple of model generations in a row where capabilities improve on benchmarks but the economic usefulness, especially for agentic tasks, basically plateaus.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fab capacity as a physical constraint, but does not say scaling past TSMC’s existing production limits would require financing new fabs and add to AI spending.

r002.rationale: It says major tech companies have enormous cash flows and can tolerate losses; it does not argue that investment substantially beyond roughly $100 billion exceeds what one committed company can readily finance.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss raising roughly a trillion dollars or the results such fundraising would require.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core of the financial bear case is pretty simple: the amount of capital going into AI right now is enormous, and it's being spent on the expectation that revenue will catch up, and that expectation could just fail.

So to put rough numbers on it, the big AI companies and the hyperscalers are now spending on the order of hundreds of billions of dollars a year on capex – data centers, chips, power. And the revenue from AI products, while it's growing really fast, is a lot smaller than that. So you've got this gap, and the whole thing is being financed on the assumption that the gap closes. If you're an investor, you're essentially betting that models keep getting better at a pace that unlocks a lot more economically valuable work, and that the companies capture a good chunk of that value.

There are a few ways that could go wrong. One is that scaling just delivers less than people hope. Maybe you spend 10x the compute, you get a model that's somewhat better, but not better in ways that translate into customers paying a lot more. The returns to scale are real, but they're logarithmic-ish, and if the economic value of "somewhat better" is also diminishing, then at some point the next order of magnitude of training compute isn't worth it.

A second failure mode is that the capabilities do arrive, but competition erodes the margins. If you've got five or six labs all roughly at the frontier, plus open-weight models that are only a bit behind, then prices get competed down toward the cost of inference, and nobody makes the kind of money that would justify the capex. You've built something incredibly valuable for the world but a bad business.

A third thing is just the timing. Even if AI ends up being hugely transformative, there's a classic pattern where the infrastructure gets overbuilt ahead of demand – the railways, the fiber buildout in the late nineties. Lots of the fiber got used eventually, but the companies that laid it went bust first. So you could have a world where AI is going to be a very big deal and there's still a serious crash, because the spending ran ahead of the revenue by a few years and the financing dried up.

And then the thing I'd flag is that this is all quite reflexive. A lot of the spending is being justified by the expectation of continued spending. The chip companies are selling to the labs, the labs are raising money on the strength of their compute, the cloud providers are building out for the labs. If investor sentiment shifts – say a couple of flagship model releases disappoint, or a big customer pulls back – you could get a fairly fast unwinding where everyone cuts capex at once. That matters for timelines too, because if the capital goes away, the scaling slows down even if the technical path was still open.

I'd say I personally put meaningful probability on some version of this. Not that AI progress stops, but that there's a period – maybe a couple of years – where the money pulls back, growth in training compute slows a lot, and progress is driven more by algorithmic improvements than by raw scale. I think that's maybe 20 or 30 percent likely in the next several years, something like that. The reason I don't put it higher is that so far revenue has actually been growing pretty fast, and the people writing the checks have been looking at the internal numbers and continuing to write them. But it's definitely one of the main ways the fast-timelines picture could fail.

r001.rationale: The response mentions spending on data centers, chips, and power, but does not identify financing new semiconductor fabs or TSMC’s production limits.

r002.rationale: It describes AI capex as hundreds of billions of dollars across large companies and hyperscalers, but does not argue that investment above roughly $100 billion exceeds what one committed big tech company can readily finance.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss raising roughly a trillion dollars or say that doing so would require impressive demonstrated results.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic bear case is that the cost of scaling keeps growing faster than the revenue you can get from the resulting systems. You can have continued improvements in capabilities without those improvements being enough to justify the next round of investment.

One version is that AI is useful, but actually turning that usefulness into revenue is slower than people expect. Businesses need to change their workflows, the systems need to be reliable, and you need ways to check their work. So you could have impressive demos and a lot of usage, but still not have enough customers willing to pay enough to support the spending.

Another version is that AI creates a lot of economic value, but the companies training the models don’t capture very much of it. If competing models are fairly close substitutes, competition could push prices down. That’s good for users, but it makes financing the next, substantially more expensive training run harder.

The key question is whether spending more gives you a sufficiently valuable advantage. If a much larger model can reliably do work that smaller models can’t, that could justify a lot of investment. If it’s just somewhat better at tasks that are already served pretty cheaply, the financial case is much weaker. So the bear case doesn’t require AI progress to stop. It just requires the returns to additional spending to disappoint.

r001.rationale: The response discusses rising scaling costs but does not mention semiconductor fabs, TSMC’s production limits, or financing new fabs.

r002.rationale: It does not mention roughly $100 billion or argue that a single big tech company would struggle to finance AI investment at that scale.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss raising roughly a trillion dollars or the need for impressive demonstrated results to do so.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic bear case is that capabilities keep improving, but the revenue you can capture doesn’t grow fast enough to justify the next round of investment.

You can have AI systems that are very useful and still have a disappointing business. There’s competition pushing prices down, there are costs to running the models, and there’s a gap between being able to do something in a demo and having a product that people reliably use and pay for. So it’s possible that a lot of the value goes to consumers, rather than to the companies training the models.

And then there’s a timing issue. You spend a huge amount up front on chips and data centres, on the expectation that future systems will unlock much larger markets. If those systems take longer to arrive, or if adoption is slower than expected, you could get a pretty substantial pullback in investment.

So I’d distinguish the claim that scaling stops producing useful capabilities from the claim that scaling stops being financially attractive. You don’t need the first for the second to happen.

r001.rationale: The response mentions spending on chips and data centres, but it does not identify financing new semiconductor fabs or TSMC’s existing production limits.

r002.rationale: It discusses large upfront investment generally, but says nothing about investment beyond roughly $100 billion or a single big tech company’s ability to finance it.

r003.rationale: The response notes that future systems are expected to unlock markets, but does not say that raising roughly a trillion dollars would require very impressive demonstrated results.
